Does there exist, for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$, a ring or field in $\mathbb{R}$ with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$?
#1154: [Er79h,p.119][Va99,2.48]
analysis
Erdős and Volkmann [ErVo66] proved that, for any $\alpha\in[0,1]$, there exists a group of real numbers of Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$.
Falconer [Fa84] proved that any subring with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha \in(1/2,1)$ cannot be a Borel or Suslin set. Edgar and Miller [EdMi01] proved that any real closed analytic subfield of $\mathbb{R}$ has Hausdorff dimension either $0$ or $1$. Later the same authors [EdMi03] proved that any subring of $\mathbb{R}$ which is Borel or analytic either has Hausdorff dimension $0$ or is equal to $\mathbb{R}$.
Mauldin [Ma16b] proved that subfields of $\mathbb{R}$ exist with Hausdorff dimension any $\alpha \in [0,1]$ assuming the continuum hypothesis.
Additional thanks to: Quanyu Tang

A partial proof 
claimed by Yi Wang (using gpt5.6sol).
 Summary:
 Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a subring such that the set
$I := \{X \in 2^\omega : \beta(X) \in E\}$, $\beta(X) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty X(n) 2^{-(n+1)}$,
is closed under the Turing join $X \oplus Y$.
$\beta$ and $\beta \times \beta$ preserve Hausdorff dimension. The join map $J(X,Y) = X \oplus Y$ gives a bi-Lipschitz equivalence between $(I \times I, \rho_2)$ and $(I, \rho)$; since squaring the metric halves the dimension.
Let $d := \dim_H(E)$, $0<d<1$, we have $\dim_H(E \times E) = 2d$.
For each $a,b \in E$, let $\ell_{a,b} = \{(x,y) : y = ax + b\}$. The family $L = \{\ell_{a,b} : a,b \in E\}$ has dimension $2d$, and each line intersects $E \times E$ in an affine copy of $E$, hence has dimension $d$. By the weak furstenburg set conjecture (arXiv:2106.03338 thm1.1),
$\dim_H(E \times E) \ge 2d + \varepsilon(d,2d) > 2d$, a contradiction. Thus $d \in \{0,1\}$.
 Notes:
 This proof was completed in collaboration between human and AI.

A partial proof 
claimed by Yongxi Lin (using GPT5.6).
 Summary:
 Assume $\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{sTD}$ (strong Turing Determinancy). Let $E$ be a subring of $\mathbb{R}$. Suppose that $d:=\dim_{\mathrm H}(E)>0$. A theorem of Peng--Wu--Yu (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.10470) states that, under $\mathsf{sTD}$, for every set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a closed set $F\subseteq A$ such that $\dim_{\mathrm H}(F)\geq \dim_{\mathrm H}(A)-\varepsilon$.
Applying this to $A=E$, we obtain a closed set $F\subseteq E$ satisfying $\dim_{\mathrm H}(F)>0$. Let $S$ be the subring of $\mathbb{R}$ generated by $F$. One may write\[S=\bigcup_{n\geq 1}\ \bigcup_{\substack{p\in\mathbb{Z}[X_1,\ldots,X_n]}}p(F^n).\]Each set $p(F^n)$ is analytic, since $F^n$ is closed and $p$ is continuous. Since there are only countably many integer polynomials, $S$ is analytic. Moreover, $F\subseteq S\subseteq E$, and hence $\dim_{\mathrm H}(S)>0.$ We can then apply the result of Edgar and Miller to conclude that $S = \mathbb{R}$.
